label: GDP growth
note: Whether the economy behind the borrowing is still expanding. Growth is what eventually pays debt down without new borrowing.

label: Reserves (import cover)
note: Months of imports the central bank could fund from its reserves. Below three is generally considered thin, and the statutory floor is four.

label: Exports / GDP
note: How much foreign currency the economy actually earns. External debt is repaid in dollars, and exports are where they come from.

label: Current account / GDP
note: Negative means the country spends more abroad than it earns there and must borrow the difference. Persistent deficits pressure the shilling.

label: Interest / government revenue
note: The share of every shilling collected in tax already committed to interest before a single service is funded. This is the measure that tightens first, and it deteriorates long before anything is missed.

label: External debt / GNI
note: Debt owed abroad, which must be serviced in foreign currency rather than shillings — so a weaker shilling makes it heavier without anyone borrowing more.

label: Debt service / exports
note: What repayment costs measured against what the country earns abroad, which is the source of the currency it is repaid in.
